en: There are many foes to fight to destruction.
Before you are Manchus:
‘He is one of those Burut,’ they say;
You have many enemies who will contend with you.
The chief of your shepherds is Oshpur.
Your Oshpur, the Black Kalmyk,
Saying, ‘Your son has turned out unruly,’
Has laid a burden upon your household.
This Altai is no land for you;
This Oshpur is no kin to you.
If you heed Oshpur,
Rich Jakyp, he will alter
Your thoughts.
Bright red crimson cloth,
When I pull its edge it will not part.
Your Kalmyk shepherd Oshpur,
If a Kyrgyz falls into his hands,
Does not seem a scoundrel who would hesitate.
Green-patterned fine silk,
When I tear its sides it will not part.
Your Oshpur, whom you hold dear,
Will slander you when a jangjung comes;
He seems no man to spare a life.
He calls his horses ‘mörün.’
Your Oshpur, whom you hold dear,
Seems no man to spare a life.
Oshpur, to whom you gave your child—
May he not dig your deep pit,
Slandering you when Kalmyks come;
May he not bring your misery to a boil.
May he not find your slightest weakness
And, telling the Chinese,
Strip you of your fearful might.
If you trust this Oshpur,
He will trouble your thoughts.
He will seize and hand over to the Chinese
Your son named Manas.
Alas, this world!
You have called Altai your land;
You have gone about calling Kalmyks your people.
This Altai is no land for us;
These Kalmyks are no people of ours.
They will steep poison in your vessels and churn,
Using this child of yours as a pretext;
These Kalmyks will bring about his end!
Scatter your countless wealth and livestock;
Taking Manas as your support,
Flee from this Altai.
If you do not flee this Altai,
They will bar the fields where your livestock graze;
They will seize the child you were granted at death's door.
If they seize you, they will slaughter you, beginning with Akbaltay;
The Manchus will beat out your far-ranging madness.
Your livestock are many, your child mischievous;
He has reached twelve.
You have no strength to restrain Manas!
The black-steel Zulpukor,
He will draw from its sheath and fight.
Your Manas will quarrel not with Kalmyks,
But with the Chinese khan Esenkan;
He will contend with him.
They will not let you turn your plow;
Your foul-tongued Black Kalmyks
Will not let you stay in Altai.
They will put your strength to torment;
Suddenly they will seize
That son of yours, Manas.
The khan's gate is Judgment Day.
When he issues a harsh command,
When he says, ‘Give me your child,’
Is there a way to enter?
Against unbelievers like black spiders,
My Khan Jakyp, hear my words,
You have no strength to struggle.
You have no support to lean upon;
You have no people settled securely,
To meet them face to face in battle,
To take firm revenge—
You have no renowned Kyrgyz people.
You have no forest to flee into;
The one you sat relying on,
Your father Khan Ogoy, is also gone.
You have no support to lean upon,
To face them and wage a battle,
To make trouble for these Chinese,
To wrest you free—
You have no renowned Kyrgyz people.
The Black Kalmyks and many Manchus,
When they surrounded us before,
When they raised a terrible slaughter,
We fled in panic and sorrow.
Those on whom we relied,
Our kinsmen, we lost.
Digging gold and sowing grain,
We have come to live in Altai.
Your son has turned out unruly;
What course shall we take now?
That is what I say—understand it.
Oh, rich Jakyp, heed my words:
To leave these unbelievers,
To reach an inheritance,
To scatter much wealth,
To flee toward the many Kyrgyz,
Never to turn toward the Kalmyks,
Never to remain in this Altai,
When horses grow fat and fit,
When men grow stout and restless,
Castrate your rams and make them wethers;
Make all your sheep fat.
Castrate your stallions and make them geldings;
Make your horses fit and swift.
Castrate the males of your livestock;
Gather your strength early.
Measure your ability to flee;
Pray above all for your son Manas's wishes.”
Chyyrdy spoke these words.
Before she had closed her mouth,
Before one could say this or that,
Before an eye could blink,
Oshpur came in a fury,
Speaking to rich Jakyp:
“Go quickly to your livestock;
Your calamity of a son Manas,
Take him into your own hands.
Load your burden on your camel;
Bear the hardship yourself.
The son Manas you gave me
Will not heed a single word;
He will not tread the path he is driven on.
He is a child who will not listen.
If that child lives,
He is one who will bring sorrow.
Breaking courts and taking spoils,
Either your son will make you rich,
Or, thrusting his chest out and raising strife,
Your son will lay you low.
The Black Kalmyks and Manchu people
Will not let you settle in Altai.
Hear my words, rich Jakyp;
This son will bring you no good.
I heard a rumor among the people:
‘Many shepherds and horse herders
He slaughtered in the fields,’ I heard.”
When rich Jakyp heard this,
His heart was troubled;
His tears poured down.
Rich Jakyp was greedy for livestock;
His heart was troubled for his herds.
His unruly son Manas
Looked utterly bad in his eyes.
Rich Jakyp grew angry
And went and mounted his horse.
Together with Oshpur,
He now went toward the sheep.
Up onto a yellow hill's spur,
Onto an overhanging point,
He rode and looked out.
In the hollow of Great Altai,
Beside a broad river,
In a hollow among uneven hills,
Where rich Jakyp's sheep lay,
Smoke rose in separate billows.
He had gathered forty children;
Of the wretched sheep left without a master,
Fully half, the hero Manas
Appeared to have slaughtered in the fields.
His frenzy had taken a firm hold;
He had devised a plan no one could fathom.
Slaughtering sheep in the fields,
He had held a feast like Ala-Too.
At the place where he spent the night,
An enduring shrine arose.
No one at twelve had ever
Behaved as this one did.
The hut erected in the fields—
Beside that hut,
Whatever person came near it,
One corner of the hut—
Manas and the forty children
Could play ordo there at ease.
If you looked at its other corner,
Eighty people could simply
Lie there with plenty of room.
At the place where he slaughtered sheep,
A shrine arose like an enclosure.
The Mustayyp spirits supported him.
Where he had circled three times,
A shrine as large as a house arose.
At that time God favored
Manas from above.
The forty chiltens and Kydyr Niyaz
On that day had become
Mighty companions to Manas.
No such soul could be created again.
If you looked at one of his aspects,
He was a blue-gray tiger crouching ready.
A black-spotted leopard
Raged at his flank.
A short-tailed, gray-maned lion
Prepared itself at his right.
From the sky, the giant black bird Zymyryk,
As if about to swoop and snatch him up,
Stretched out its great sprawling feet.
His protectors were one nine;
Making Manas loom mightily,
They were supporting him then.
His world was in balance;
He was the lion supported by Shay.
The youngest of six lions,
He was God's beloved servant.
Your Manas had gathered forty children
And set up tremendous games.
Of Khan Jakyp's many sheep,
He had slaughtered fully half.
The needy poor and wandering dervishes
Had eaten their fill through Manas.
All those who had eaten their fill
Had named Manas a lord.
He had begun an extraordinary fancy;
Of the many sheep Oshpur tended,
He had slaughtered half.
Rich Jakyp was greedy for livestock,
An utter fool who understood nothing;
That wretch was a heedless man.
Grieving and sorrowing, he said:
“My Manas, born for ruin,
You have drained my strength.
Why have you slaughtered in the fields
My livestock held by the enemy?”
Then Manas said this,
Telling a marvel no one knew:
“Alas, father, what are you saying?
Making ownerless livestock numerous,
What do you gain by keeping them?
What inheritance will you attain?”
Manas spoke, standing small and straight;
Rich Jakyp stood rejoicing.
Before he had closed his mouth,
Before rich Jakyp had stilled his anger,
God forbid we see such a face!
Mottled-gray pennants, red standards,
A tumult of ‘Boy, boy!’
Moon-crested black standards,
A tumult of shouting.
Beyond the Manchus,
On this side of Kanggay,
Esenkan's envoy,
The Black Kalmyks' and Manchus'
Land warden who guarded the land,
Had heard a tale from a gossip:
‘The Kyrgyz Burut Jakyp's
Many herds that are not turned back
Have eaten up the land,’ he heard.
Taking seven banner standards,
Taking about seven hundred troops,
The chief of the seven hundred,
